prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice clocks, from the magic-wavelength concept to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is the clearest case before us of a result that is both conceptually new and quantitatively robust. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift of the trapping field and lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once. Ye's group then showed systematic uncertainty and stability at the 10^-18 level, with many-body (spin-exchange) physics inside the clock. Several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) now reproduce this performance and compare clocks against each other, so this does not rest on a single measurement. The consequences are concrete: a redefinition of the second is under discussion, relativistic redshifts can be seen over millimetres, and there are bounds on drifting constants and dark-matter couplings. A two-name configuration is compact and defensible, and the achievement is distinct from the frequency-comb prize of 2005 and the ion-control prize of 2012. Measurement of time itself is fundamental, and it is not a technology-first prize, even though applications will follow.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty and credit. Optical frequency metrology and single-ion control have already been recognised (Hall and Hansch 2005, Wineland 2012), so a sceptic can call the lattice clock an incremental refinement of a recognised programme. The credit set is wider than two people: Ludlow, Bloom, Kitagawa, Lemonde, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups all contributed to reaching 10^-18. There is also a real chance that the committee prefers a discovery that reveals something unexpected in nature over an instrument that is superbly well characterised. I rate my own subfield highly here, and I cannot rule out bias toward precision atomic physics.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first because of the clarity of the metric, the field-opening impact and the independent reproduction, but notes that ion-clock work was recognised earlier and other clock groups are not credited.
responses.response: I agree on the metric, and I think that is the decisive point: stability and accuracy are quoted in the same units by competing laboratories, and the numbers agree. I accept his caveat about ion clocks, but the lattice scheme is a different physical route. It gets its statistics from many atoms and it needs the magic wavelength, which is a concept from atomic structure theory and not a refinement of Wineland's single-ion methods. I would still keep the citation worded around the lattice scheme so that it does not appear to claim the whole of optical clocks.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the clock only eighth. She accepts the two-person configuration but argues that novelty is constrained by the 2005 and 2012 prizes and that the benefit to humanity is currently modest.
responses.response: This is the most serious disagreement with my own ranking, and I take the novelty point seriously. The answer I would give is that 2005 recognised the comb as a ruler and 2012 recognised control of single quantum systems, and neither delivered a clock with a million-fold gain in counted atoms and a stability that lets one resolve a gravitational potential across a laboratory bench. On benefit, I would reverse her argument: it is not yet a tool for daily use, but when the laser was invented its uses were also unclear, and I would not weigh the 'broad benefit' criterion as heavily as the clear experimental discovery. I do accept that her preference for NV centres rests on a field that has had broader practical use so far.

responses.point: Eriksson puts magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first: a theory prediction followed by a decisive experiment, with a new quantum behaviour in a material and many reproductions, and with a real allocation question over Cao and Fatemi.
responses.response: I defer to him and to Mehlig on condensed matter, and I do not dispute that flat-band correlated phases opened a large field; it is my first alternative. My reservations are about maturity and about attribution. The origin of the superconductivity is still debated, so the stable interpretation that I look for is not there yet, and the early-career experimentalists who did the key work are not among the credited names. In the lattice clock the credit set is clean and the physics is understood, which is why I place it above moire matter, but I would not be upset to see the committee choose B031 if the attribution can be settled.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as foundational quantum optics that became the platform for superconducting processors, a natural successor to the 2025 prize, but admits that four credited names exceed the three-person limit.
responses.response: I agree that circuit QED is important, but the proximity to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits seems to me a larger obstacle than he suggests. Two consecutive prizes in superconducting circuits would be hard to defend in the public discussion of what the committee is rewarding. The four-to-three problem is also an unresolved attribution issue, since leaving out Blais or Girvin is a judgement the record does not settle. I would also ask whether, in the circuit-QED case, the discovery is the architecture or the downstream processors.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the lattice clock fourth: a clean two-laureate configuration that is mature and reproduced in several laboratories, with the second's redefinition pending. His own first place is gamma-ray burst afterglows.
responses.response: I thank him for agreeing that the clock configuration is clean and that its neighbouring prizes concerned different things. On the afterglow discovery, I defer to him on astrophysics, but the attribution looks harder to me than for the clocks: the late van Paradijs and the optical groups are central to the redshift measurement, and the credited trio omits them. If the committee can resolve that credit I would regard it as a serious claim.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see the lattice clock as new enough given the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize
Whether Katori and Ye are the right pair or whether Ludlow, Bloom or the ion-clock groups should share the credit
How the committee weighs a measurement advance, whose payoff via a redefinition of the second is still pending, against a discovery of new quantum behaviour
Whether the 2025 circuit prize makes any related quantum-circuit candidate harder to justify now
The maturity of moire flat-band superconductivity, on which I defer to colleagues in condensed matter
statement.conflict_note: Possible connection to flag: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund attosecond group and with Ursula Keller's group at ETH. None of these is among the credited names for the shortlisted candidates, so no specific recusal issue is apparent from the provided profile. I work on atomic many-body theory and on theory for storage-ring and attosecond experiments, which is adjacent to B029, B044 and B018, and the committee should note that when weighing my enthusiasm for those candidates.
